impact_innovation.summary: A brain implant powered by AI helped a father with ALS speak nearly two million words over two years. Casey Harrell can now talk with his daughter, crack jokes, and keep working — in a digital version of his own voice.

impact_innovation.title: AI is helping save eyesight before it is lost
impact_innovation.summary: AI is catching diabetic eye damage before patients even notice vision changes. A quick retinal scan during a regular diabetes visit can flag disease on the spot — no separate appointment needed. A Johns Hopkins study shows it's already working in pediatric clinics.
impact_innovation.extended_summary: You can see perfectly fine and still have damage silently building at the back of your eye. That's the terrifying reality for people with diabetes — and by the time vision changes show up, the window to intervene may already be closing. AI is changing that. In some clinics, a staff member snaps photos of the retina during a routine diabetes visit, and an authorized AI system reads them on the spot. If something looks wrong, the care team arranges a specialist exam immediately. A randomized Johns Hopkins study of 164 young people with diabetes put the approach to the test. The software doesn't treat the eye — it just makes the first step impossible to skip.

impact_innovation.summary: A Provo startup turned down investor money because the guy wanted them to make their kids' tablet more addictive. Instead, Scribbi's e-ink device treats a child's mistakes as data — quietly flagging patterns for parents without ever telling a kid they got it wrong.
impact_innovation.extended_summary: An investor sat across from Katarina and Keller Seamons with a simple pitch: make your kids' tablet more addictive and it'll be worth way more. They said no. That refusal is the whole point of Scribbi, the Provo startup's e-ink tablet built to be put down. When their daughter writes her S's backwards, most software would mark it wrong — Scribbi quietly flags the pattern for a parent and helps her fix it without ever telling her, in the moment, that she failed. It's a small design choice that flips the entire logic of kid-tech: a child's mistakes are information worth noticing, not noise for an algorithm to correct.

impact_innovation.title: CA Researchers Identify Odors That Repel Honeybees From Pesticides
impact_innovation.summary: UC Riverside researchers found chemical compounds that safely repel honeybees from pesticide-treated crops. Using a machine-learning model, they screened over 50 million compounds to find scents that push bees away — potentially saving pollinators from toxic exposure.
impact_innovation.extended_summary: Honeybees have over 200 odor receptors, which makes finding a scent that repels them — rather than attracts them — incredibly difficult. But that's exactly what researchers at UC Riverside just pulled off. Biologist Anandasankar Ray's team built a machine-learning model trained on chemical structures and real bee behavior, then screened more than 50 million compounds to find ones that safely push bees away from pesticide-treated crops. The goal isn't to harm bees — it's to redirect them, keeping them out of fields where pesticides could devastate their colonies. With pollinator populations in decline worldwide, a scent-based deterrent could be a genuine game-changer for agriculture and the bees that keep it running.

impact_innovation.summary: The Wiyot Tribe just cut the ribbon on 39 units of housing for young people who are homeless or close to it — built inside a former office building, a Victorian, and two new ADUs. Native youth get priority, and applications are already open.

The Wiyot Tribe cut the ribbon on Jaroujiji Youth Housing, converting the old building into dozens of one- and two-bedroom units — plus a Victorian next door, two new accessory dwelling units, and a renamed house called Abalone House. In total, 39 units: 31 for permanent housing for 18-to-24-year-olds, seven for short-term shelter for 16-to-18-year-olds, and an apartment for the manager. Kitchens and living rooms are shared.
